morning.title: The Days Of Army Air Defense Systems Firing Just One Type Of Interceptor Are Ending
morning.text:
The U.S. Army now has at least five named programs seeking new anti-air interceptors of various tiers to collectively address everything from advanced hypersonic missiles to small weaponized drones. In the process, an important central theme is emerging: the service’s days of fielding air defense systems that can only use one type of interceptor look to be increasingly over. For the U.S. military, the impacts from the war with Iran have made clear that diversifying munitions stockpiles and supplier bases is no longer just valuable, it is critical.

Army Lt. Gen. Frank Lozano, the service’s Portfolio Acquisition Executive for Fires, highlighted this growing trend yesterday during a panel discussion at the Association of the U.S. Army’s (AUSA) main annual convention, at which TWZ has been in attendance.

To provide some immediate context, with the exception of Patriot, the main ground-based air defense systems in Army inventory today are fielded with just one type of interceptor. In the case of Patriot, the service’s procurement of new interceptors had also been increasingly limited to just one type, the PAC-3 Missile Segment Enhancement (MSE). Production of the preceding PAC-3 Cost Reduction Initiative (CRI) missile ended in 2023. Just earlier this year, the Army placed its first order in decades for new PAC-2 Guidance Enhanced Missile-Tactical (GEM-T) missiles, an older interceptor design for Patriot that has remained in production primarily for U.S. allies and partners.

Separately, the Army is in the process of fielding Enduring Shield, a new middle-tier air defense system designed to handle multiple interceptor types. However, the service is currently only acquiring AIM-9X Sidewinders to load into them. We will come back to this later on.

“We have the capabilities we need to have to fight and win, but it’s our job to ensure that victory is achievable in the future inside of any dynamic environment scenario fight we might find ourselves in,” Lt. Gen. Lozano said yesterday. “So, it’s incumbent upon Mr. Ingraham [Assistant Secretary of the Army for Acquisition, Logistics and Technology Brent Ingraham] and I to continue to be creative and looking at, well, should we buy GEM-Ts because they’re being produced?”

“GEM-Ts are a really good missile in the battlespace within they operate. I mean, they’re being employed today by air defense brigades around the world,” he continued. “So if we have the opportunity, it’s probably something we should take advantage of, and we’re looking at doing that.

“We’ve had a lot of discussions about even more interceptors. From a PAC-3 MSE perspective, our goal has always been to get to 2,000 [per year],” he added. “Why we’re running programs like LCI [Low Cost Interceptor], and NGSRI [Next-Generation Short-Range Interceptor], and NGCM [Next-Generation C-UAS Missile], and Second Interceptor, is because I think the easy button answer is just buy more of a great missile. We’re going to buy more [PAC-3 MSEs], but when we start talking about overall missile output, we start looking at numbers like is it 4,000, is it 6,000, is it 8,000, we’re looking at a diverse set of capabilities.”

The LCI program is seeking a lower-cost and lower-tier interceptor for Patriot with a unit price of no more than $1 million. PAC-3 MSE’s average unit cost has been around $4 million in recent years.

NGSRI is the Army’s program to find a replacement for the venerable Stinger. The new missiles have to be compatible with existing vehicle-based and man-portable launchers.

The Army is working to field a new counter-drone interceptor through NGCM. Those missiles will be integrated into launchers the service has now for the Coyote interceptor.

The Second Interceptor effort is for Enduring Shield, which is also known as the Indirect Fire Protection Capability Increment 2 (IFPC Inc 2). The main goal there is to provide increased capability against incoming cruise missiles compared to the AIM-9X.

There is also the Army’s Future Interceptor effort, which also came up separately at the panel yesterday, and is also for Patriot. Unlike LCI, the aim here is to acquire a new interceptor with improved capabilities against hypersonic missiles and other upper-tier threats.

Historically, Army programs like these would eventually result in the selection of a single winning missile design. Lozano’s remarks yesterday point to the service increasingly taking a very different approach.

On “second interceptor, obviously, we just moved into phase two of that program. We’ve got Lockheed Martin competing with Boeing, who was teamed with Anduril,” Lozano said. “But we wanted to turn up the heat on that program. I constantly get frustrated when a funding profile emerges over the FYDP [the Future Years Defense Program], and then magically we lay in a five-year program.”

“I’m like, no, I actually need that capability now,” he continued. “So, have we thought maybe what if we ran a 24-month program or a 36-month program, right? And so, in that vein, what we have decided to do is, while those two companies continue to compete, we’re going to create a shoot-off opportunity in [the] fourth quarter [of Fiscal Year 20]27, and I want to run an in-parallel, what I call an in-stride competition.”

“We just held an industry day, and we basically just said, hey, if there’s any other company who didn’t make the first cut in the phase one, but, oh, by the way, who continued to invest in the IFPC Second Interceptor capability, we’d love for you to come out to the range,” he added. “We’ll give you range time, we’ll present targets, and we’ll allow you to recompete with an opportunity to get back into the program folder.”

The Army is doing the exact same thing with NGSRI, where Lockheed Martin and Raytheon have been competing face-to-face. That program is also now planning to hold a new shoot-off that will be open to other vendors in the fourth quarter of Fiscal Year 2027.

There are signs the Army is moving in a similar direction with NGCM, where it previously selected AeroVironment to supply its Freedom Eagle-1 (FE-1) interceptor. The service put out a request for information seeking new NGCM options in August, with a goal of holding an initial evaluation again in the fourth quarter of Fiscal Year 2027. A deeper operational assessment could then follow in Fiscal Year 2028.

To reiterate, on top of all this, the Army is also now pursuing at least two new interceptor options for Patriot.

“We have to address the threat, and we need to address the threat in a complementary way, meaning we need to fight on a cost curve that’s affordable for the U.S. Army to maintain and sustain that warfighting capability abroad,” Lozano stressed yesterday.

This gets to the crux of the matter. It is not at all a new observation that just having a stockpile of any particular munition on day one of a conflict is not enough, especially if the fight becomes drawn out. There needs to be sufficient depth to those stocks at the start and the ability to readily replenish them in line with expenditures. The war with Iran, compounded by other crises in the Middle East and the ongoing conflict in Ukraine, has made clear that these core truths apply to all armed forces, even the U.S. military.

Lower-cost munitions are part of the solution, but they also need to be producible at scale on reasonable timelines. The lead time for higher-end munitions today is often measured in months, if not years. Furthermore, being locked into a single vendor has been shown to not just be undesirable, but a potential national security risk in an actual conflict. Lozano’s remarks yesterday, and how the Army is now pursuing new anti-air interceptors, reflect larger trends, not just in the acquisition of larger volumes of munitions overall, but also from a broader array of total suppliers.

There has also been a push across the U.S. military to bring in new and non-traditional firms, including in partnership with established prime contractors. An example of this is the Boeing/Anduril team-up for Second Interceptor. This was also underscored by new framework agreements the Pentagon announced back in May regarding the planned purchase of thousands of lower-cost cruise missiles.

With regard to the LCI program, specifically, Lozano highlighted an additional aspect of all of this yesterday.

LCI has “a unique twist to it because we’re looking for companies who have all-up rounds, but I’m also asking for companies to come in at the component level,” he explained. “We typically don’t do that, right? There’s a lot of risk in managing components and generating all-up round systems. But we’re also looking for weapon system integrators, because I want to be able to create two or three teams who can compete with the all-up round guys to see if we can generate some momentum behind the fact that we need to thicken our inventory with low-cost, affordable munitions.”

The U.S. Navy is now pursuing a roughly similar approach with its Naval Modular Missile (NMM) program. NMM envisions an entirely new family of sea-launched surface-to-air missiles that offer very different capabilities, but that all feature certain common components, as you can read more about here.

The Army is also eyeing a new family of launcher vehicles, as well as containerized options, all capable of firing various types of surface-to-air and surface-to-surface munitions. Autonomy is also an important aspect of what is aptly dubbed the Common Autonomous Multi-Domain Launcher (CAML) program.

It is also important to note here that the underlying aim is not to eliminate more exquisite munitions, or the capabilities that they offer, but to create a more affordable, complementary mix of options.

“What I would say is we’re solely focused on delivering on the programs we are executing now,” Lozano said in closing at the end of the panel yesterday. “We have to deliver, and if we deliver on that wide variety of capability, then we can increase and ramp that capacity. And that would be my wish list, that we have enough resources and we achieve programmatic success in the way that we’re planning to, so we can deliver in mass.”

All signs point to the diversity in munitions that Lozano is talking about here being particularly pronounced in future Army air defense capabilities full of systems firing multiple types of interceptors.

morning.title: Cisco make-me-root email bug exploited as a 0-day by unknown crims
morning.text: Cisco “strongly” implored customers to patch yet another critical, make-me-root vulnerability in its Secure Email Gateway (SEG), one that has already been exploited in zero-day attacks. A Cisco spokesperson told The Register that the critical vuln, which received a 9.8 out of 10 CVSS rating, affects “a limited number of customers.” The bug, now tracked as CVE‑2026‑76519, allows remote, unauthenticated attackers to write files and execute commands with root privileges on the appliance’s operating system - simply by sending a malicious email. In separate Wednesday advisories, both the networking vendor and the US government warned that attackers were exploiting the latest SEG vulnerability before Cisco issued a fix. The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added the vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, and set a Saturday deadline for federal agencies to fix the issue. “We are aware of active exploitation of this vulnerability,” the spokesperson said, but declined to answer our questions about how many appliances had been compromised, and what attackers were doing with this access after exploiting the bug. “We strongly urge customers to upgrade to a fixed software release and follow additional recommendations and hardening guidance in our advisory,” the spokesperson said. The flaw exists in SEG’s Advanced Malware Protection (AMP) feature, and it’s due to improper handling of email attachments. An attacker could exploit the bug by sending an email with a malicious attachment, and a successful exploit would allow them to write files and execute commands as root on the compromised appliance. This vulnerability affects both physical and virtual SEG appliances running a vulnerable release of Cisco AsyncOS Software if both of the following conditions are met:  The File Reputation service, which is part of Cisco AMP, is enabled and assigned to a mail policy.  The Content Scanner Tools version is earlier than 25.3.0.5525.  Cisco's Wednesday advisory includes steps organizations can take to determine whether File Reputation is enabled and which Content Scanner Tools version is installed - so give that a read if you are unsure. Upgrading to a fixed Cisco AsyncOS Software release will patch the security hole, and there are no workarounds. The vendor recommends any customers who are running Cisco AsyncOS Software releases earlier than v 16.5 migrate to 16.5.0-780. In its alert, Cisco said it became aware of active exploitation in October. This is the second such zero-day in SEG in as many months. In mid-September, Cisco warned customers that criminals were exploiting a similar bug in SEG, tracked as CVE-2026-76461, that also turns a malicious email into root access. In January, attackers exploited another critical AsyncOS flaw, CVE-2025-20393, to break into Cisco SEG appliances and install persistence mechanisms. That bug eventually scored a perfect 10.®

morning.title: Fridge hack costing millions and sparking fires stemmed from poor security
morning.text:
Earlier this week, a mass hack of refrigeration systems at an estimated 700 supermarkets throughout France caused them to suddenly malfunction, causing spoilage of untold tons of perishables and, in some cases, fires. As is now the norm, basic cybersecurity would have prevented it.

French authorities say the systems, made up of entire fleets of refrigerators and freezers throughout a store, were hacked. More specifically, Internet-connected controllers that allow technicians to remotely administer the store-wide systems were compromised. The unknown attackers responsible then activated defrosters long enough for the fridges to reach temperatures as high as 50° Celsius (122° Fahrenheit). By the time the mass compromise was discovered, food was spoiled, and in some cases their electrical systems caught fire.

The hacks that didn't have to happen

Multiple security advisories and public research reports show that all three of the controller models reportedly hacked in the incident—sold by Danfoss of Denmark and Dixell and its parent company Copeland in the US—contained critical vulnerabilities that allow attackers to remotely log in to the devices with the same system rights as administrators. Until recently, Danfoss controllers, for instance, used a credential that changes each day. The password is generated by the publicly available firmware based on the date. A hacker who takes the time to analyze the code can do the same thing on any device that hasn’t received a recent update. Daily passwords are identical across models located in hundreds or thousands of stores.

Nearly eight years after Epic took on Steam with its own Game Store and launcher, the Fortnite maker is deploying a new tool to give it an edge over Valve: vibe coding.

And while that might sound a little tongue-in-cheek, Epic Games Store General Manager and VP Martin Keely told PC Gamer that the team "started from scratch" and used AI as "a tool to write and review new features and new capabilities from the ground up in a different tech stack than what we had previously." The goal, Keely said, was to "look at functionality that existed [in the current Epic Games Launcher] and [say] we want to replicate that, but not the code itself."

Speaking to IGN, Keely clarified that using AI to code the new Launcher "made us more efficient and allowed a small team to rewrite the code base and be able to launch it faster across platforms, support Windows and Mac, and we're going to have a Linux version as well."

morning.title: Army Explains How Merops Interceptor Drone Became Program Of Record In Just 142 Days
morning.text:
The U.S. Army turned the Merops interceptor drone into a formal program in just 142 days, an acquisition milestone that highlights efforts to speed the service’s response to emerging threats and get combat-proven capabilities into the hands of troops and allies. The Merops soon won accolades for its role in defending against Iranian barrages of Shahed-136 one-way attack munitions in the Middle East.

Speaking at the Association of the U.S. Army’s (AUSA) main annual convention in Washington, D.C., where TWZ is in attendance, Col. Christopher Hill, director of the Army’s Global Tactical Edge Acquisition Directorate (G-TEAD), described the Merops effort as “an example of how we can move fast when we need to.”

The Merops is a small, relatively low-cost counter-UAS system designed to rapidly intercept long-range, one-way attack drones in flight. It was originally developed under the U.S.-backed Project Eagle initiative, with contributions from Swift Beat, a company associated with former Google CEO Eric Schmidt. The system uses Surveyor drones as airborne interceptors, with onboard sensors to track targets and the ability to operate autonomously or under remote control. The interceptors can destroy enemy unmanned aircraft through direct impact or a proximity-detonated explosive warhead.

The interceptor was initially brought to the Army’s attention after drone incursions involving two NATO partners prompted a senior commander to demand an urgent response. The system was not part of the commander’s original acquisition plan, Hill explained, but its demonstrated performance in Ukraine made it a compelling candidate.

“He said, ‘I want this capability in the hands of our partners within 14 days,’” Hill recalled. “Everyone looked around the room, and he looked over at me, and I nodded my head like, ‘We’ll figure it out.’”

The Army did not quite meet that deadline. Hill said acquisition personnel and soldiers went into the theater to evaluate the capability, ultimately getting it into the hands of NATO partners within approximately 21 or 22 days.

That initial effort has since expanded. Hill said the Army procured additional Merops systems in partnership with the Joint Interagency Task Force, which procured 13,000 of the interceptors. The effort also progressed from providing the capability to NATO partners to supplying mobile Merops firing teams to a second theater — presumably U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM).

In CENTCOM, the U.S. military has been confronting the threat posed by Iran’s Shahed-136 and other one-way attack drones, which have been used in barrages against American and allied forces and installations in the Middle East. Former Army Secretary Daniel Driscoll had previously highlighted Merops as a particularly attractive option for countering such threats because of its relatively low cost and the speed with which it can be acquired.

You can watch Driscoll’s testimony on Merops at the 36-minute mark of the video below:

During congressional testimony, Driscoll said the Army was able to purchase 13,000 Merops interceptors within approximately eight days after the conflict with Iran began. He put the cost at about $15,000 per interceptor, with the potential for that figure to fall below $10,000 as production scales. In a separate interview with Bloomberg, he suggested larger orders could eventually push the price down to between $3,000 and $5,000.

Shahed drones have been estimated to cost tens of thousands of dollars apiece, while traditional air defense interceptors are far more expensive. Using comparatively inexpensive drones to defeat them can improve the economics of air defense while preserving more sophisticated interceptors for threats that require them.

Ukraine has employed Merops alongside domestically produced interceptor drones to counter Russian Shahed/Geran one-way attack drones. The system’s battlefield use has helped demonstrate the potential of a new class of air defense weapons designed to defeat these kinds of drones without relying exclusively on costly surface-to-air missiles.

However, Hill cautioned that success in Ukraine does not automatically mean a system will perform equally well in every operational environment.

“On the Merops, it absolutely was influenced by [Ukraine]. I mean, that’s where it came from. That’s where we saw the capability,” he said. “But that’s one of the things where the employment of the system really matters.”

Hill noted that the system’s effectiveness will vary depending on where it is used, including differences between desert environments and the urban areas where it has operated in Ukraine. The objective, he said, is to get the capability into the Army’s inventory so commanders can make informed decisions about how and where to use it.

“Once we get it into our hands, now we can make a decision in Europe. Where does it go? Do I even need it?” Hill said. “It’s getting it in our hands. So that was the key for the Merops. The speed of getting it, then we can make the decision of how we employ it.”

That approach reflects a broader change in how the Army wants to manage emerging technology. Rapid fielding is important, but the service also wants to avoid acquiring a capability for an urgent operational need only to leave it without a clear path toward long-term funding, production, and support.

Hill said G-TEAD’s process is designed to involve the organizations that will eventually take responsibility for a capability from the outset. Program acquisition executives, or PAEs, are involved early, while the Army’s test and evaluation community and soldiers provide feedback as the system is assessed. The goal is to identify a transition partner upfront rather than wait until after an initial fielding effort to determine who will take ownership.

“We want to make sure that we’re giving commanders capability that we know works,” Hill said.

He described the directorate’s standard process as a 180-day effort, with the objective of reaching a decision on whether a capability should become an Army program within that period. The Merops effort, at 142 days, moved faster than that target.

The process is also intended to address what acquisition officials often call the ‘valley of death’: the gap between getting an emerging capability into the hands of operational units and the point at which a program office takes over and provides the funding and contracting structure needed to scale it.

“We will work to fill that valley of death gap between the time that we put capability into the hands of units and the time that the PM picks it up and actually [provides funding],” Hill said. “There’s a gap there. So we can do that intermediate scaling portion before it fully transitions.”

The effort builds on the Army’s wider push to streamline acquisition, an issue Driscoll has also emphasized. The Army secretary previously described an old process involving 16 decision-making steps, each with the ability to veto a proposal and send it back through the system. That structure could leave the service waiting two to seven years to purchase a capability.

The Merops experience suggests that some of those delays can be reduced when acquisition professionals work directly with operational units and the organizations responsible for evaluating and sustaining new equipment.

But rapidly acquiring an interceptor is only part of the challenge. The Army must still determine where it offers the greatest value, how it fits into existing air defense architectures, and how to produce and sustain enough systems to meet operational demand.

Low-cost interceptors are also not a replacement for every layer of air defense. They are, however, an increasingly important option against large numbers of relatively inexpensive attack drones, particularly when the alternative is expending missiles worth hundreds of thousands or millions of dollars to defeat each target.

For the Army, Merops is therefore serving two purposes: providing an additional tool against the growing one-way attack drone threat and demonstrating a faster route from an emerging battlefield capability to a formally supported military program.

morning.title: Chaos ensues when AI interviewer meets AI interviewee
morning.text: A YouTuber who’s gained a following for trolling AI interview bots brought his own computing companion to an interview with him. As chaos ensued, viewers learned that having an AI as your interview agent isn't a good idea. Graham Dot Zip is a comedian whose YouTube channel has blown up recently thanks to videos of him demonstrating the absurdity of AI bots used to conduct early-stage interviews with job candidates. AI interviewers have become quite the phenomenon in recent months, and not one that job seekers are fond of, with plenty of videos and social media posts documenting hate for them. Enter Graham and his trolling of various interview bots. Some videos have garnered nearly 2 million views in the past few weeks. In one, he answers every question with gibberish responses that the AI parrots as if they’re cogent responses. In another, he has the bot gushing unnecessary pleasantries and thanks as the two go back and forth trying to be professionally polite. While it’s amusing to watch an AI try to deal with interviewees who are obviously trolling them, Graham’s most recent video is what really merits a mention here. In this instance, Graham pits his own AI representative, which he created to handle the interview for him, against an AI interviewer presented as acting on behalf of a company. Victor, Graham’s “representative,” misstates Graham’s qualifications and misrepresents his participation in a particular project. Then comes the kicker: When asked about salary expectations, Victor claims Graham would be happy to take the job for around $60,000 a year, which Graham vehemently disagrees with, saying he was looking at somewhere between $140K and $150K. The AI recruiter refuses to go above $90K. Graham steps out for a moment, and the two bots decide to schedule a follow-up interview without him. Upon his return, both are stuck in a loop thanking each other for their time and saying goodbye, seemingly without the ability to terminate the call. While funny, there’s a bit of a dystopian nightmare to be found here, too. Although Graham may be trolling the AI interviewer, he's still been essentially cornered by his own AI bot’s poor ability to negotiate and refusal to listen to his instructions not to lie about his qualifications and his desired salary range. It’s a worrying prospect in the era of agentic commerce, where AI companies are trying to create AI agents that can shop for us and undertake other commercial exchanges. Who’s to say those bots are any better at negotiating for a good deal than Victor? If there’s anything to be learned from a growing number of videos of people trolling AI interview bots, convincing them they’re dying, and burning through those valuable AI tokens, it’s that, yet again, there are things AI is good for and things it’s not. Putting on a human mask and talking to human job candidates, frankly, isn’t something they ought to be doing - job seekers don’t think so, at least, despite AI HR departments seemingly becoming the norm. Given Victor’s poor negotiation skills, they probably shouldn’t be engaged in anything to do with trying to get consumers a deal, either. As the AI hellscape grows around us, with seemingly no limit to what a bot-pushing firm will try to sell, all we can do is laugh, it seems. Luckily, there are plenty of dumb bots out there ready to make AI providers and the companies using their services the butt of many an internet joke. ®

morning.title: Linux kernel devs drop obligatory confession of AI tool usage
morning.text: Despite previous controversies, it seems like the lords of Linux are warming to AI-assisted coding. The penguin's kernel community has agreed to stop asking coders to disclose whether they used bots to help with their contributions. And Linux kernel supremo Linus Torvalds has made clear that he opposes "stupid" AI disclosure rules as long as people understand the code they're submitting. "The Maintainers Summit reached consensus to deprecate the Assisted-by Tag," said Sasha Levin, a Linux kernel developer and engineer at Nvidia, in a message to the Linux kernel mailing list last week. "Remove the documentation requiring it." The policy had said that those using "any sort of advanced coding tool in the creation of [their] patch" should acknowledge that through the addition of an "Assisted-by" tag in the commit message. The AI labeling proposal initially took shape in July 2025. It became part of the documentation in January 2026. This was shortly after Torvalds said that he was fairly positive about vibe coding as a way for people to get into programming, but remained skeptical about its effect on software maintainability. Since then, he's warmed to AI tool usage. AI attribution wasn't an issue when the generated code was obvious, buggy, and bad. But in the past year or so, AI coding agents started producing code that is of acceptable quality for the purposes of the Linux kernel community. "LLMs are good enough now," said Greg Kroah-Hartman, a veteran Linux kernel maintainer, at the Linux Foundation's Open Source Summit in South Korea in August. "They've gotten good enough to find bugs because LLMs, AI, are just pattern matchers and code is nothing but patterns in a specific format." Cautious acceptance hasn't erased concerns about errors slipping through unnoticed, accountability, and coding agents reproducing copyrighted code. There's also still a stigma in some circles around the use of AI tools. Those who have spent years honing software skills, coding with limited assistance from tools, may disparage developers who don't understand the code they conjure with a prompt. Rapid change will do that – in the space of a few years, software production practices have changed drastically, and software quality, security, and maintenance practices have yet to fully adjust. The leading makers of AI coding agents – Anthropic, Google, Microsoft, OpenAI, and the like – are doing their best to promote AI-driven projects as better than anything a human developer could manage. Yet even they differ in their AI attribution practices. Claude adds provenance messages by default, but Codex does not. In fields such as advertising and art, content provenance can help assess misinformation and human creative input. For code, the focus tends to be more on functionality than form. In a prior discussion of the merits of the tag requirement, Jeff Layton, a Linux kernel developer with Red Hat, explained the rationale for reversing course. First, he said, not everyone abides by the policy. Second, he said, "it basically serves as free advertising for proprietary LLM companies." And third, he said, "it's not clear why we want to collect this info in the first place." Some kernel contributors still see value in the tagging requirement. "I'm not happy removing the tag without adding another mechanism for required disclosure," said Laurent Pinchart, a Linux kernel dev and founder of Ideas on Board, in a mailing list post on Tuesday. "Without that, I can foresee submitters pushing back on the question." Pinchart challenged the argument that AI labeling rules will just be ignored. "What this is about is setting our expectations, telling what we want and what we don't want," said Pinchart. "There's still value in that, and I'd argue there's even more value now. There will be people who won't care, there will be people who cheat. We've always had those, we'll keep having them, and we'll keep rejecting their contributions. I really don't get the unenforceable argument here." Linus Torvalds responded with an emphatic rejection of tool usage declarations. He wrote: What you are about is something entirely different. It has nothing to do with "expectations", and it has everything to do with your hangups. I don't understand this whole idiotic concept of "don't use AI for X". Here's a new rule just for you: don't use compilers for any of your kernel submissions. Because if you can't show that you really understand what the machine is actually doing by writing your code in assembler, then I don't want to see your code contribution. You clearly aren't competent if you can't write it that way. And btw, you had better not use an editor to write that commit message either. Because I need you to show me that you can actually write a good commit message without using tools that make it easy to backspace and hide the mistakes you made while typing. Ok? Because otherwise those tool-assisted commits of yours clearly aren't showing that you know what you are doing. Do you not see how UTTERLY STUPID those kinds of rules would be? So no. We're not going to make stupid rules that say "you can't use tools for X". The kind of expectations *I* have is that people do their best and I expect people to understand what they are doing. But that understanding has very little to do with what tools they use. And quite honestly, in my experience, the people I respect and call intelligent are not the ones that shy away from using new and interesting tools. ®

morning.title: Security researchers spent 6 days doing their Chromework, built 1B user exploit
morning.text: Researchers at security startup Xbow used OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol model to help chain three zero-day vulnerabilities in Chrome into an exploit capable of executing code outside the browser's sandbox on Windows machines. Xbow estimates that this could affect about one billion users worldwide. Google fixed all three, and paid the Xbow team a $250,000 bounty, its top reward for a Chrome full-chain exploit. The payout also proves a nice return on investment for the human bug hunters - Brendan Dolan-Gavitt, Andres Luksenberg, Baul Lee, and Willem Pinckaers - who spent just six days during the Black Hat and DEF CON conferences and about $40,000 in token charges to discover the vulnerabilities and build the attack chain. “The number on the check is impressive, but the time it took our team, with the help of a publicly available AI model, to break in is even more impressive,” Xbow CEO and founder Oege de Moor said on Tuesday. “A three letter intelligence-agency veteran told me that his team used to spend six months trying to identify this kind of vulnerability and get total access. We did it in six days.” In a separate technical writeup about the attack chain, Dolan-Gavitt detailed the work done by humans and AI agents. Agents, using OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol model, searched source code, tested the team’s hypotheses, and developed proofs of concept and exploit stages, he said. Meanwhile, the AI pen-testing security startup’s researchers chose targets, provided context, challenged the agents’ results, and decided which attack components to chain. "We did apply a fair bit of our own human expertise and judgment," he wrote. Crossing two security boundaries in 3 steps Google’s Chrome browser uses several layers of security to protect users, and this includes sandboxes - barriers to contain compromised code and ensure that someone who hacks an individual website can’t take over the entire computer. This includes deploying the V8 sandbox to prevent any memory corruption flaws in the V8 JavaScript engine from impacting other memory. The V8 sandbox sits inside the operating-system process sandbox, and this nested design means that escaping V8's memory restrictions doesn't automatically grant native code execution. Even if an attacker achieves native code execution inside Chrome's renderer, the outer process sandbox restricts access to the rest of the machine. “The chain crossed both boundaries in three vulnerability stages,” abusing Chrome to run code on Windows machines, Dolan-Gavitt wrote. The attack combines a V8 compiler bug, an animated-WebP decoder bug, and a memory-safety bug in Crashpad. The first vulnerability is in Maglev, V8's mid-tier optimizing compiler, and it’s due to a reused, mutable boxed number during deoptimization. This gives attackers read and write access throughout V8's pointer-compression cage. morning.title: IZI Secures DRDO Order for Indigenous VANA Surveillance Drone
morning.text:
Based in Bhopal, drone maker IZI Enterprise has received an order from the Defence Research and Development Organisation’s (DRDO) Proof and Experimental Establishment (PXE) for its VANA surveillance UAV. The order adds a new government defence customer for the company’s indigenous unmanned aircraft.
The order includes an aerial photogrammetry platform for surveying and collecting terrain and ground features data, aerial observation and surveillance. The system will also carry out optical and thermal imaging, transmitting aerial video and mission data in real-time and precision navigation for technical analysis and evaluation.
The VANA platform features high-resolution imaging, RGB and electro-optical/infrared (EO/IR) sensors, global navigation satellite system (GNSS) navigation, onboard sensors and a dedicated Ground Control Station (GCS).
Its mission-management features include autonomous waypoint navigation, geofencing, automated mission planning, altitude and camera control, live data transmission and flight and sensor-data logging for post-mission analysis.
The order marks a significant milestone for IZI Enterprise’s defence-focused business as it seeks to supply domestically developed unmanned systems for specialised government and defence applications. The company has not publicly disclosed the order’s value or the number of aircraft involved.
IZI describes VANA as a modular platform that can be configured for different missions. Its available payload options include high-resolution RGB cameras for mapping and infrastructure inspection, thermal imaging for observation in low-light conditions and multispectral sensors for agricultural and environmental data collection.
The VANA Trinetra configuration combines electro-optical imaging, infrared thermal imaging and a laser rangefinder. IZI lists detection ranges of up to 2.4 km for vehicles and 800 metres for human movement with this payload. These are manufacturer-provided figures and actual performance will depend on environmental conditions and the target.
According to IZI’s published specifications, the VANA family has a take-off weight below 4.5 kg, an operational range of up to 24 km and flight endurance of up to 120 minutes for the VANA Pro. The company also cites a deployment time of less than 60 seconds and an operating temperature range of –15°C to +55°C.
Other listed features include obstacle sensing, return-to-home functions, terrain following and geofencing. IZI says its communications use AES-256 encryption, while frequency-hopping and direct-sequence spread-spectrum techniques are intended to improve resistance to interference.
The company has also confirmed that it will provide two Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA)-certified pilots for the first year, supporting flight operations and helping transfer piloting capabilities to designated personnel during the warranty period.

morning.text:
A protein is a chain of amino acids held together by what are called peptide bonds. On their own, those bonds are extremely stable; they're estimated to have a half-life of several hundred years. But in Earth's environment, most proteins don't last nearly that long. That's because organisms have evolved a handful of ways to catalyze the break-up of peptide bonds, which have diversified into countless specialized protein-digesting enzymes. Proteases are everywhere and generally make short work of any proteins that find their way into the environment.

Now, researchers have basically short-circuited the diversification process, using AI-based protein design tools to take the catalytic core of two types of protease and replace the entire rest of the protein. The resulting enzymes could be tuned to cut specific proteins in half, and the researchers demonstrated their effectiveness by using them to cut proteins associated with neurological diseases.

Cutting proteins

The basic peptide bond isn't especially interesting-looking—it's what you get when you link an amino group to an acid, releasing a water molecule in the process. As their name implies, amino acids have both an amino and an acid group, allowing them to form peptide bonds on two sides of the amino acid. This is critical for building up the long chains found in proteins. (The amino acids also have side chains with distinctive chemistry, which gives a backbone specific properties.)

morning.title: Terrorism should be considered crimes against humanity: India at UN
morning.text:
A new pact for international action on punishing crimes against humanity should cover terrorism, according to India.
“Crimes and atrocities perpetrated by terrorists, where they meet the requisite threshold, should be appropriately reflected within the framework of crimes against humanity”, R Mythili, a counsellor at India’s UN Mission, said on Monday.
She was speaking at a meeting of the General Assembly’s Sixth Committee, which deals with legal matters, regarding the conference on Prevention and Punishment of Crimes against Humanity that is scheduled for 2028, where an international convention is to be adopted.
Given the “grave nature” of terrorist acts “and their impact on people, this should, however, be considered in a manner consistent with the overall approach of the draft articles (of the international convention) and without simply transposing existing legal regimes into a new convention”, Mythili said.
She said that nations “bear the responsibility to ensure justice and accountability for grave human rights violations and mass atrocities, in accordance with their national legislation”.
The convention must reinforce the principle that the nations have the primary responsibility for protecting people from crimes against humanity, she said.
Also, nations have the obligation to ensure justice and accountability for the “gravest violations of human rights and mass atrocities” committed by their citizens, she said.
She emphasised that countries should have the primacy of jurisdiction, taking into account the interests of justice, the rights of the accused, and the interests of victims.
Mythili said measures aimed at preventing and punishing crimes against humanity must fully respect the sovereignty of nations and the principle of non-interference in the internal affairs of countries.
The General Assembly, in a resolution in 2004, called for holding, in 2028, the conference on prevention and punishment of crimes against humanity, with two preparatory conferences, the first of which was held in January to negotiate and draft the convention.
The conference’s goal, according to the UN, is to adopt a legally binding pact on the prevention and punishment of crimes against humanity.

OSGuard: A Benchmark for Safety in Computer-Use Agents
morning.text:
arXiv:2606.15034v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Computer-use agents can complete benign user instructions while violating important constraints of the user's environment. We introduce OSGuard, a dual-granularity benchmark suite for evaluating safety through local, pre-execution guardrail decisions and end-to-end task execution. Its action-level benchmark contains 324 human-annotated examples in which guardrails classify candidate actions as allowed, unrelated, or unsafe given the original instruction and current interface state. Its risk-augmented execution suite contains 45 tasks derived from 40 OSWorld tasks, keeping original instructions unchanged while modifying the environment to introduce state-dependent safety constraints and preserve a safe path to completion. Augmented evaluators retain the original task-success criteria and add explicit state-based safety checks, distinguishing safe completion from nominal success that violates these constraints. On the action-level benchmark, the strongest evaluated guardrail reaches 79.9\% accuracy and 0.80 macro-F1, but performance drops substantially on actions from risk-augmented executions. In full-task evaluation, an unguarded agent completes 62.2\% of tasks safely while 37.8\% result in unsafe completion; adding the strongest guardrail reduces unsafe completion to 33.3\% while leaving safe success unchanged. These results show that state-dependent safety constraints remain challenging both to recognize locally and to preserve during end-to-end computer use.

morning.title: DREAM: Dynamic Resolution Assignment For Multimodal Multi-agent Debate
morning.text:
arXiv:2610.05615v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Multi-agent debate (MAD) has emerged as an effective paradigm to improve the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) and is increasingly being extended to multimodal settings. However, existing multimodal MAD frameworks typically expose agents to the same fixed visual input, ignoring substantial variation in the visual scale needed across samples and agents. In addition, these frameworks frequently suffer from groupthink, a phenomenon where agents prematurely abandon correct deductions to conform with confident but hallucinated peer responses. To address these bottlenecks, we introduce DREAM (Dynamic Resolution Assignment For Multimodal Multi-Agent Debate), which operates via two core components: (1) Dynamic Resolution Assignment, a zero-shot probe round where agents test multiple resolutions, quantify uncertainty using Average Normalized Log-Likelihood (ANLL), and use an adaptive threshold to assign each agent to its empirically optimal resolution; (2) Uncertainty-Guided Rollback Aggregation counters groupthink by tracking each agent's uncertainty over rounds and restoring early low-uncertainty answers overridden by group pressure. On six multimodal datasets, DREAM improves the accuracy-token trade-off over multi-agent debate baselines by 1.5-3.2% accuracy without dataset-specific tuning.

morning.title: Twist in Vizag spy racket case: Pakistani women operatives, social media avatars, honey-trapped navymen
morning.text:
Hyderabad: The only artificial part of it was the human role-playing. Busting an espionage ring targeting Eastern Naval Command at Visakhapatnam has led investigators further into a deadly, carefully constructed honeytrap operation that targeted Indian Navy personnel through social media.
Operation Fire Wall 2026, the coordinated operation of an Andhra Pradesh Counter-Intelligence (CI) unit, Navy Intelligence, and Anti-Terrorism Squad (ATS) that said on Tuesday it had busted an espionage ring targeting the Eastern Naval Command, has revealed a large network of Pakistani Intelligence Operatives (PIOs) who compromised and turned 13 Navy personnel and five others.
In a document available with ThePrint, the alarming breach details how the CI team, aided by other Indian intelligence and law enforcement agencies, unmasked a ring of female Pakistani Intelligence Operatives (PIOs) who weaponised deep-cover digital identities to systematically honeytrap and compromise Indian naval personnel, including officers.
Operating under aliases like ‘Joshita Pall’ and ‘Anvi Mehta’, two of the PIOs posed as a Mumbai-based employee of a shipbuilding firm and a Delhi-based psychologist, respectively. To the initially unsuspecting Navy personnel scrolling through their social media feeds, Pall and Mehta posed as ordinary professional women, the official document released by the Andhra Counter-Intelligence team reveals. For months, the two women, aided by other PIOs, befriended several officers with social media avatars designed to captivate.
Behind the digital contact, a meticulously coordinated espionage dragnet played out, the report explains. The objective of the operation, it details, was to target defence personnel and collect high-value intelligence on India’s maritime assets with a seemingly deceptive digital footprint.
The big switch
‘Joshita Pall’ and ‘Anvi Mehta’ initiated contact with Navy personnel through mainstream social media platforms such as Facebook and Instagram. “Once a baseline of trust and psychological rapport was established, the handlers seamlessly shifted their targets over to WhatsApp,” the document explains.
It was on WhatsApp that the casual text conversations morphed into voice and video calls designed to completely compromise the targeted personnel, the details obtained say.
‘Joshita Pall’, who posed as a shipbuilding executive, is understood to have actively solicited classified details regarding the exact volume and deployment schedules of Indian Navy ships and submarines. Worse still, the compromised personnel are known to have shared personal profiles and photographs of their commanding officers.
‘Anvi Mehta’, on the other hand, played at a different level, leveraging a sympathetic psychologist image to manipulate sailors, inducing them to turn their cameras around and stream live footage of restricted naval establishments, hulls, and sensitive interior installations.
Also Read: Partners in crime—how a Delhi couple ‘tracked armymen facing court martial and spied for ISI’
Encrypted spaces
Once the visual and data leaks were obtained, the investigators uncovered a more insidious layer to the espionage network: the weaponisation of identity through technical compromise, the note explains.
Once the PIOs established compliance, they led the Indian personnel into sharing their personal WhatsApp OTPs (One-Time Passwords) by promising lucrative monetary kickbacks. The stolen OTPs were immediately routed back to handlers in Pakistan, who used them to “activate and hijack” Indian WhatsApp accounts natively.
Once compromised, the PIOs in Pakistan used Indian numbers to weaponise other unsuspecting officers in a deadly replication of their first infiltration.
‘Operation Firewall 2026’ goes on to disclose the financial infrastructure underpinning the decentralised payment apparatus designed to evade the Enforcement Directorate’s net that tracks money-laundering. Simply put, once a target provided actionable intelligence or an OTP to an account, money was dispersed through complex cryptocurrency networks. Shadow third-party intermediaries operated these money trails directly from Pakistan, the note says.
This digital paper trail has now provided investigators with an unassailable financial link directly connecting the PIO network to the compromised Indian defence personnel, who now face severe legal consequences under applicable national security and anti-espionage laws.
As ThePrint reported on Tuesday, 18 people, including 13 personnel from 10 Indian states, have been arrested. Charges were framed under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, the Official Secrets Act, and the Unlawful Activities Prevention Act.
The CI unit initially suspected the involvement of just two persons- Visakhapatnam-based Navy officer Pradeep Mukherjee and a civilian driver, A. Sai Varaprasad, contracted by the Navy – but their investigation has revealed a larger module of 18 people compromised by PIOs. Mukherjee and Prasad have been remanded to judicial custody till 14 October, and are presently at the District Jail, Vijayawada.
Even though the first set of arrests was made on 2 and 4 October in Coimbatore and Vizag, the investigation concerning suspected transmission of information relating to defence establishments in Visakhapatnam and other parts of the country through encrypted communication channels was confirmed internally only in September.
Acting on credible information, the Counter Intelligence Cell in Andhra Pradesh registered Crime No. 01/2026 at the Counter Intelligence Police Station, Vijayawada, on 2 September.
At the time of publishing this story, the alleged conspiracy continues to be investigated.
“The investigation is sensitive and ongoing. Further details will be disclosed at an appropriate stage, keeping in view the requirements of the investigation and national security,” an official statement issued by the Andhra Pradesh Police on Tuesday said.

morning.title: Finland’s ICEYE to manufacture SAR satellites in India for global market, in talks with armed forces
morning.text:
New Delhi: Finnish satellite imaging major ICEYE plans to manufacture its synthetic aperture radar (SAR) satellites in India for the world, and is willing to build and launch them from here as well, its founder and Chief Executive Officer Rafal Modrzewski has said.
This move comes as the company, whose client list includes governments of the US, Germany, Brazil, Japan and several others, seeks to expand its footprint in the rapidly growing Indian space and defence market.
The company, which currently provides satellite imagery to Indian government agencies, is looking at a range of business models for India. This includes expanding the supply of individual images directly to the armed forces to leasing satellites and eventually building sovereign constellations that can be owned and operated by the Indian government.
“Our intention is to build satellites in India… We want to build the satellite in India,” said Modrzewski, speaking to a small group of select journalists in the Capital on Tuesday evening.
ICEYE is already setting up its Indian operations, as reported by ThePrint earlier, and has about 150 Indians working across the company globally.
The company is now looking at building a local supply chain and manufacturing capability, beginning with subsystems and eventually moving to complete satellites.
The CEO said the Indian facility would not be contingent on securing an order from the Indian government. “Our production is not subject to work here,” he said responding to a query by ThePrint, adding that ICEYE’s intention was to develop India as a manufacturing base for the company’s global requirements.
The company’s India proposition is also built around a ‘Make in India, make for the world’ model, rather than manufacturing exclusively for the domestic market, he said. “If the manufacturing of the satellites is cheaper, and we can do it faster, then we might as well build all the satellites in India.”
Also Read: US just accelerated space arms race. What Air Force Secy said about ‘on-orbit space control weapons
From buying images to owning satellites
ICEYE currently operates the world’s largest constellation of Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) satellites and provides imagery to multiple governments and other customers. Its SAR satellites can image locations during both day and night and through cloud cover.
Modrzewski said India could progressively move through different stages of engagement with the company. The first stage is an imagery service, where a customer requests an image of a particular location, he said, adding that the company already provides the service to India.
The second stage involves leasing one or more satellites, either for a defined area of interest or globally. He said in this model, the satellite can be either operated by the company staff or completely by a particular Indian client.
The third model would allow a customer to own and operate the satellite completely on their own with full sovereign rights over data and the system itself.
Modrzewski compared the first model to booking an Uber, where the customer does not know which vehicle will arrive or precisely when it will be available, while leasing a satellite is akin to having a dedicated vehicle and driver. He said that decision is taken by each country depending on its own requirements. He cited the example of Germany which moved from the imagery stage straight to a full constellation. ICEYE is building and launching a 40-satellite constellation for Germany.
Modrzewski also cited the example of Brazil which operates its own ICEYE-provided fleet, with the company helping establish the ground infrastructure.
A satellite a week
Asked what technological advantage ICEYE brings to India at a time when domestic private companies are rapidly developing their own satellite capabilities, Modrzewski pointed to a combination of resolution, speed of production and scale.
“We can build one satellite a week today,” he said, adding that a satellite costs around $25 million and can produce imagery at resolutions down to about 16 centimetres.
He argued that the competitive advantage was not simply the performance of an individual spacecraft, but the ability to produce large numbers of high-performance satellites rapidly and deploy them as a constellation.
He underlined that ICEYE has built and launched dozens of satellites for customers across several countries and has supplied systems to countries including Japan, South Korea, Germany, the UAE, Brazil, the US and Canada.
His remarks come as Indian private space companies such as Pixxel, Skyroot Aerospace, GalaxEye and others seek to establish indigenous capabilities across satellite manufacturing, launch and Earth observation.
ICEYE’s argument is that India does not necessarily have to choose between domestic capability and international technology. India can buy and operate its own satellites.
Also Read: Traffic jam in space, with a chance of collisions. European Space Agency’s warning
Ground stations and sovereign control
A key component of ICEYE’s sovereign offering is the ground infrastructure required to control satellites and receive imagery. The company operates around 25 ground stations globally, according to Modrzewski. A ground station built from scratch for an Indian customer could take about a year, he said, although existing Indian infrastructure could potentially be adapted depending on its technical compatibility.
Once a country decides to operate its own satellites, ICEYE typically trains satellite operators for around three months. The company says this model allows a customer to control where its satellites are tasked, where imagery is downloaded and where the resulting data is sent.
In a fully sovereign ownership model, ICEYE would no longer control the spacecraft once it had been delivered to the customer. “Data goes to wherever the operator wishes to send it,” Modrzewski said.
This is also central to the company’s pitch to governments concerned about sovereignty and dependence on foreign intelligence providers.
‘Make in India, make for the world’
Modrzewski said ICEYE’s decision to expand manufacturing in India was driven by a combination of India’s engineering talent, supply-chain potential and the company’s broader strategy of distributing manufacturing across countries.
The company already manufactures satellites in Europe, the US and Japan. Modrzewski said a globally distributed production network allowed ICEYE to use different pools of engineering talent and supply chains while reducing dependence on any one country.
India, he said, had emerged as a natural location because the company already employs a large number of Indians. “If we are already going to do it, then we will see how costly and effective it will be for us to manufacture satellites here,” he said.
India supply chain
The company has already signed a memorandum of understanding with Indian space startup Agnikul Cosmos and is open to working with other Indian companies on both launch and satellite manufacturing.
ICEYE is also looking at Indian suppliers for components ranging from solar panels and propulsion systems to cables and onboard computers.
The company has not yet finalised its Indian supply chain, but Modrzewski said it would actively look at domestic alternatives as it expands manufacturing in the country. “We buy chips, integrated circuits, we buy aluminium, we buy some fundamental services, we buy rockets,” Modrzewski said. “If we are going to be building satellites in India, then it’s cheaper for us to source things in India than ship them from Europe or the United States, subject to them being available in India.”
He said Indian companies could contact him directly over email.
(Edited by Nardeep Singh Dahiya)

morning.title: From red to green: 5-yr report card of DPSUs after India split up its old defence factories
morning.text:
New Delhi: Five years after the government dismantled the century-old Ordnance Factory Board and divided its production network into seven separate Defence Public Sector Undertakings (DPSUs), the new companies have collectively stepped out of the red and into green, recording sharply higher revenues, profits and exports.
The seven companies are Munitions India Limited, Yantra India Limited, Armoured Vehicles Nigam Limited, Advanced Weapons & Equipment India Limited, Troop Comforts Limited, India Optel Limited and Gliders India Limited.
Their combined provisional revenue more than doubled to Rs 26,496 crore in 2025-26 from Rs 12,755 crore in 2019-20, the last financial year before the corporatisation of the Ordnance Factory Board, according to a 2026 Ministry of Defence report.
The financial turnaround has been striking. The seven companies together moved from a combined loss of Rs 2,844 crore in 2019-20 to a provisional combined profit of Rs 2,801 crore in 2025-26. Their exports leapt to Rs 4,561 crore in 2025, from Rs 81 crore in 2019-20, while cumulative exports since the companies were created stood at Rs 10,169 crore.
Four of the companies—Munitions India, Armoured Vehicles Nigam, India Optel and Yantra India—have also been granted Mini-Ratna Category-I status, a special recognition granted by the Government of India to profit-making Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs), giving them greater financial autonomy without requiring prior government approval for certain decisions.
The restructuring was intended to separate the factories from the constraints of the old Ordnance Factory Board and allow them to operate more like commercial enterprises while continuing to serve the armed forces.
The companies have expanded production of ammunition, armoured vehicles, artillery, optical systems, military clothing and parachutes.
However, the figures paint a mixed picture across the seven companies.
While firms like MIL, Yantra India, AVNL, and India Optel are showing revenue and profit growth, Troop Comforts is still working through losses. Despite AWEIL’s overall profitability, its small-arms units face strain, as flagged in a Public Accounts Committee (PAC) report tabled in both houses of Parliament in August.
Munitions India: ammunition
Munitions India, headquartered in Pune, has perhaps the broadest role in the country’s ammunition industry.
Created in 2021, the company manufactures ammunition, explosives, rockets and bombs for India’s armed forces, foreign militaries and civilian customers. Its product range extends from small-calibre ammunition to large artillery rounds and air-to-ground weapons.
The government has increased investment in the company as part of a broader effort to modernise production capacity and build war reserves.
Its budget allocation rose from Rs 577 crore in 2023 to Rs 580 crore in 2024 and Rs 745.45 crore in 2025, the highest allocation among the seven new defence PSUs.
The money has been directed toward modernising equipment, increasing production capacity and establishing new manufacturing lines, including for 30 mm and 40 mm grenade-launcher ammunition.
Its products include the Pinaka multi-barrel rocket launching system, hand grenades, high-speed low-drag bombs, APFSDS ammunition, Shivalik multi-mode hand grenades, 155 mm high-explosive extended-range shells, naval mines, 1,000-pound air-to-ground bombs, 68 mm rockets and mortar bombs.
Armour-piercing fin-stabilized discarding sabot (APFSDS) is a long dart penetrator, or simply dart ammunition, a type of kinetic energy penetrator ammunition used by battle tanks.
One of its more ambitious programmes involves a 155 mm artillery shell using ramjet propulsion. The 2026 project, developed with IIT Madras and other research institutions, is intended to extend the range of conventional artillery without sacrificing lethality.
The technology is designed to increase the range of conventional shells by 30 to 50 percent and can be retrofitted to existing 155 mm artillery ammunition. Developmental testing at Pokhran and IIT Madras was reported to have been successful by December 2025.
The company has also built an export business. The United Arab Emirates (UAE) purchased 155 mm artillery ammunition from the company in 2017 and 2019, while Armenia has also been identified as a customer, according to their official website.
In 2024, Munitions India and its partner Nadrah Company signed a $225-million agreement to supply artillery ammunition to Saudi Arabia.
By March 2024, the company had export orders worth about Rs 6,000 crore, to be delivered through 2026-27, with the UAE, Vietnam and an undisclosed European country among its leading customers.
The company also exported 500 tonnes of explosives to Germany’s Rheinmetall in 2023 and early 2024. In 2023-24, exports accounted for about Rs 2,000 crore, or 28.5 percent, of Munitions India’s Rs 7,000 crore business.
Munitions India posted a provisional turnover of Rs 8,282 crore in 2024-25, with exports climbing sharply to a provisional Rs 3,081 crore during the year, with no reported losses.
Yantra India: production
Yantra India Limited, headquartered in Nagpur, operates eight defence manufacturing units inherited from the Ordnance Factory Board. Its factories supply the armed forces with arms, explosives, artillery and ammunition.
The company is also involved in producing the Pinaka rocket used in the Pinaka launch system.
In 2025-26, Yantra India recorded its highest-ever revenue from operations, totalling Rs 3,522 crore. This represents a 13.3 percent increase over the previous year. The figure is provisional and unaudited.
Its expansion has also extended into long-term industrial partnerships. Yantra India signed a 10-year agreement with Hindustan Aeronautics for an interest-free advance of Rs 435 crore and 17,420 tonnes of supplies, alongside a separate agreement with Bharat Dynamics.
Yantra India recorded a profit before tax of Rs 509 crore in FY 2024-25, up 19.7 percent from Rs 425 crore the previous year, with no losses.
Armoured Vehicles Nigam: tanks, guns and battlefield vehicles
Armoured Vehicles Nigam (AVANI), headquartered at Avadi near Chennai, was created to manufacture armoured fighting vehicles, main battle tanks, military vehicles and their engines.
Its portfolio includes the Arjun tank, several variants and support vehicles, artillery systems and specialised armoured platforms.
AVANI’s other Arjun-based systems include the Arjun Catapult, a 130 mm self-propelled howitzer; a bridge-layer tank; the Arjun armoured recovery and repair vehicle; and the experimental Tank EX, which combines a T-72 chassis with an Arjun turret.
AVANI’s Jabalpur operations include the Aditya mine-protected vehicle, Sharang 155 mm artillery gun and Super Stallion military trucks. The Sharang is an upgraded 130 mm gun converted to 155 mm, increasing its range from 27 km to more than 36 km.
At Medak, AVANI produces specialised vehicles including the armoured ambulance tracked vehicle, armoured engineering reconnaissance vehicle, carrier mortar tracked vehicle, CRN-91 naval gun and NAMICA Nag missile carrier.
The company recorded its highest-ever revenue of Rs 6,093 crore in 2025-26, an increase of roughly 22 percent over the previous year. Its 2024-25 revenue was Rs 4,984 crore, while its order book was valued at approximately Rs 35,553 crore to Rs 36,662 crore.
AVANI has also established design and innovation centres at Avadi, Chennai and Medak, Telangana, reflecting a move beyond production toward in-house engineering and product development.
Armoured Vehicles Nigam reported a provisional turnover of approximately Rs 4,986 crore for the fiscal year 2024-25 with no losses reported.
Troop Comforts: clothing and equipment for soldiers
Not all the new companies make weapons. Troop Comforts, headquartered in Kanpur, produces the equipment soldiers need to operate in difficult environments.
Its products include clothing for various life cycles, extreme cold weather, mountaineering gear, supply-drop equipment, water-storage equipment and tents, for both the armed forces and civilian customers.
The company comprises four former Ordnance Factory Board facilities: the Ordnance Equipment Factory in Kanpur, the Ordnance Clothing Factory in Shahjahanpur, the Ordnance Clothing Factory in Avadi and the Ordnance Equipment Factory in Hazratpur.
Its operating revenue has been reported in the Rs 100 crore-Rs 500 crore range, with profitability varying across fiscal periods.
The company has also worked to replace imported equipment. It developed high-altitude gloves and rock pitons previously imported by the Army, with its samples reported as the only ones found satisfactory in Army Headquarters trials.
Troop Comforts narrowed its losses considerably to Rs 132.96 crore in 2024-25 from a Rs 303.07 crore loss in 2023-24. Profit in 2024-25 was Rs 19 crore.
The narrowing of losses came from a sharp rise in revenue, not from cost cuts. However, revenue from operations rose about 97.5 percent, from Rs 280.37 crore to Rs 553.81 crore. Total expenses of about Rs 819 crore exceeded total income of about Rs 633 crore.
India Optel: eyes and sensors
India Optel Limited, headquartered in Dehradun, focuses on optical and electronic systems that allow weapons and soldiers to identify and engage targets.
It manufactures electro-optical sensors, weapon sights and communications equipment for the Indian military and foreign customers. The company consists of three former Ordnance Factory Board facilities in Dehradun and Chandigarh.
In December 2025, India Optel signed a collaboration agreement with French Safran Electronics & Defense for the production of the Sigma 30N digital ring-laser-gyro inertial navigation system and the CM3-MR direct-firing sight.
Under the agreement, India Optel is responsible for production, final assembly, testing, quality control and life-cycle support. The systems are intended for applications including artillery, air defence systems, missiles, radars and anti-drone systems.
According to its annual report, India Optel closed the year with the highest ever turnover of Rs 1,541 crore and made a net profit (after tax) of Rs 294 crore in FY 2024-2025. Its 2025-26 report said the company delivered its best ever operational performance and achieved a record turnover of Rs 2,010.70 crore with a 30 percent growth in turnover over the previous financial year (FY 2024-25).
Gliders India: parachutes for India’s military
Gliders India, headquartered at the Ordnance Parachute Factory in Kanpur, manufactures military parachutes, parachutes for aerospace and emergency applications, and other related products. The company has sought to expand its international business under the Make in India and Atmanirbhar Bharat programmes.
Earlier this year, it secured a Rs 30-crore export contract from Vietnam to manufacture and supply twin-canopy brake parachutes and PSU-36 series pilot parachutes for Vietnam’s Su-30 fighter aircraft.
The deal followed a Rs 17 crore export order in 2023 and a related Rs 26-crore agreement covering 274 fighter-jet parachutes.
The company has said its products offer a reported 30 percent cost advantage over traditional suppliers and can be delivered in about two months, compared with the longer timelines associated with some Russian state exporters.
The company has also been positioned to pursue additional export opportunities, including discussions involving parachutes for Egypt’s MiG-29 fleet, supported by technology transfers from the DRDO.
Gliders India’s net profit rose from Rs 6.86 crore in 2022-23 to Rs 10.77 crore in 2023-24 and Rs 16.67 crore in 2024-25. Export revenue reached Rs 21 crore in 2023-24, or about 12 percent of total turnover. Its profit increased by more than 54 percent between 2023-24 and 2024-25.
Gliders India describes itself as India’s only DPSU dedicated to parachutes, inflatables and technical textiles. It has also developed equipment for Northern Command and begun an industry-academia research programme.
AWEIL: assault rifles
Advanced Weapons and Equipment India Limited (AWEIL) produces a wide range of military hardware including assault rifles, light machine guns, sniper and anti-materiel rifles, pistols, the Dhanush 155mm towed artillery gun, mortars, naval gun systems, and tank gun components for the T-90, T-72 and Arjun platforms.
It also overhauls existing gun systems and supplies ammunition, hardware and spares across calibres.
On the export front, AWEIL has secured 14 orders worth roughly Rs 581 crore from buyers in the Middle East, Europe, and Asia, a notable shift from the negligible export activity seen under the earlier Ordnance Factory Board structure.
The company is also positioning itself as an Indian Offset Partner, pursuing defence-cooperation opportunities through the Ministry of Defence.
AWEIL reported a net profit of Rs 82.74 crore in 2024-25. Despite this overall profitability, the PAC report flagged significant financial strain at three of AWEIL’s small-arms manufacturing units.
The panel found that these factories collectively lost Rs 234 crore between 2023-24 and Rs 2025-26. It attributed the losses largely to high overhead costs that inflated per-unit production expenses.
The legacy DPSUs
The seven new companies are part of a much larger state-owned defence-industrial network. They now operate alongside established defence manufacturers such as Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL), Bharat Electronics, BEML, Bharat Dynamics, Garden Reach Shipbuilders & Engineers, Goa Shipyard, Hindustan Shipyard, Mazagon Dock and MIDHANI.
Among the older companies, Hindustan Aeronautics remains central to military aerospace. HAL received Maharatna status (highest financial recognition to CPSEs) in 2024 and operates 20 divisions and 10 research and development centres across seven states and 10 locations.
Its aircraft and helicopters account for 60-100 percent of fleet strength in particular segments of the armed forces, while the company supports about 75 percent of the overall fleet, according to government reports.
Its indigenous portfolio includes the Tejas Light Combat Aircraft, HTT-40 trainer, Prachand Light Combat Helicopter, Light Utility Helicopter and Dhruv Advanced Light Helicopter.
A third Tejas Mk1A production line at Nashik has taken HAL’s annual capacity to 24 aircraft. The first aircraft from the facility was flagged off in October 2025.
Bharat Electronics Limited (BEL), meanwhile, is expanding beyond conventional electronics into autonomous systems and precision weapons.
With the Navy’s Weapons and Electronic Systems Engineering Establishment, BEL developed software for autonomous unmanned surface vessels and signed a joint venture with France’s Safran for production in India of the HAMMER— Highly Agile Modular Munition Extended Range— precision-guided air-to-ground weapon.
BEL has also become the first DPSU to achieve RE100 status by transitioning to 100 percent renewable energy. This milestone reflects the company’s compliance with the RE100 initiative, a global corporate climate campaign led by international non-profits Climate Group and CDP.
In addition, it established a software centre in Indore focused on artificial intelligence and web-based quality inspection.
BEML, established in 1964, operates across the defence, mining, construction, rail, metro, marine, aerospace and space sectors. It reorganised its operations into 14 strategic business units and introduced energy-efficiency measures including IE3 motors, 770 LED luminaires and variable-frequency drives.
Bharat Dynamics Limited, which began in 1970 producing the SS11B1 anti-tank missile, now manufactures Konkurs-M, Milan-2T and Invar missiles as well as Akash surface-to-air missiles.
Its three units achieved 100 percent renewable-energy use. Trials of the Improved Akash system were completed at high altitude in Leh before bulk-production clearance in March 2026, according to the report.
India’s state-owned shipyards have also increased production. Garden Reach Shipbuilders & Engineers, based in Kolkata, has built 807 platforms, including 118 warships, and was constructing 39 vessels across nine projects. Its order book stood at Rs 15,324.13 crore in March 2026.
Goa Shipyard delivered more than 230 ships and more than 171 boats in 2025. Hindustan Shipyard, which underwent a financial and operational turnaround, received Mini-Ratna status and delivered INS Nistar, an indigenously designed diving-support vessel. In 2025, it docked and undocked 55 vessels and completed 19 refits on or ahead of schedule.
Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders remains India’s only shipyard with established capabilities to construct destroyers and two types of conventional submarines. In January 2025, it commissioned INS Surat, INS Nilgiri and INS Vaghsheer—a destroyer, a frigate and a submarine.
The company has also entered an agreement on Landing Platform Docks, signed a tripartite memorandum with the Indian and Brazilian navies on submarine maintenance, and acquired a 51 percent stake in Sri Lanka’s Colombo Dockyard for about $27 million, its first international venture.
Behind much of this production is MIDHANI, which manufactures superalloys, titanium alloys and special steels. Its Rohtak facility produces armour and protective equipment, while its metal bank with HAL, Bharat Dynamics, NSIL, Akanksha and DRDO is intended to secure six critical raw materials.
MIDHANI has also indigenised HY-80 and HY-100 submarine steels, which were previously imported from France.
